intro: This guide takes your group through David Livingstone (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It’s written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. It follows the Scottish mill boy who became a doctor, missionary and explorer in Africa, and it tells his story honestly: his courage, his faith and his promise-keeping, but also his blind spots, the cost his choices laid on his wife and children, and the many Africans whose courage and skill made his journeys possible.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close in prayer (2–3 minutes), in your own words or by turning the chapter’s closing “One thing to do this week” into a prayer together, and leave that challenge with the group for the week ahead.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself first and look over the activity; most weeks need nothing more than paper and pens. This book doesn’t look away from hard things: a lion attack, the cruelty of the slave trade, a massacre, racism, the deaths of Livingstone’s wife and eldest son, and the loneliness of a family left behind. Let teens weigh his failures as well as his faith, without turning the sessions into either a trial or a tribute. Some in your group may know family hardship, an absent parent or grief at first hand, so keep personal reflection private, follow up gently with anyone who seems troubled, and point them to a parent, pastor or other trusted adult.

weeks.summary: David Livingstone grows up in one room in Blantyre, goes into the cotton mill at ten, and works from six in the morning to eight at night for ten years, studying at night school and reading a book propped on his machine. The mill gives him endurance and respect for working people, but also a habit of judging everyone by how hard they work and despising those who can’t keep up. The big idea: God sees both the work and the worker, and working hard is not the same as working for God.

memory_verse.text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.

activity.title: Hard Work or Working for God?
steps: Draw a line down the middle of a sheet of paper and label the two sides “Working hard” and “Working for God.”
As a group, list what can drive each one: for example, wanting to be admired, fear of failing, love for others, gratitude to God.
Read Colossians 3:23 aloud and ask what changes when work is done for the Lord rather than for people.
Ask: why might a hard worker like Livingstone find it difficult to be patient with people who can’t keep up?
Have each person write down privately one person they tend to be impatient with, and one way to help them this week.

weeks.summary: In his late teens Livingstone takes the gospel personally, and a book by Thomas Dick shows him that studying creation can be a kind of worship, so he no longer has to choose between his Bible and his questions. He trains as a doctor and joins the London Missionary Society, but nearly fails his probation; once his mind goes completely blank in the pulpit, though a fellow student remembered him carrying an injured woman to safety on a dark road. The big idea: a weakness doesn’t disqualify you, because God gives each person gifts for the work he has for them.

memory_verse.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.

activity.title: Gifts and Gaps
steps: Give everyone a sheet of paper folded in half.
On one side, have each person write privately one thing they find hard that others seem to find easy, such as speaking up or making friends.
On the other side, have them write one thing they can do, however ordinary it seems.
In pairs, tell your partner one strength you have noticed in them.
Ask the group: how did God use Livingstone even though he never became a good preacher?

weeks.summary: With China closed by war, Livingstone heads for southern Africa, lives among the Bakwena to learn Setswana properly, and concludes that Africa will be reached mainly by African Christians. At Mabotsa a lion seizes him, and Mebalwe, a Christian teacher, runs at it with a gun that fails and is mauled himself; Livingstone recovers at Kuruman and marries Mary Moffat. The big idea: God often rescues and uses us through other people, and those who help us deserve to be named and thanked.

memory_verse.text: But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion’s mouth.

activity.title: The Unnamed Heroes
steps: Ask the group to think of a famous achievement, from sport, history or science, that one person usually gets the credit for.
As a group, list the people who made it possible but are rarely named.
Reread the part of the chapter about Mebalwe and ask why the old retellings often left him out.
Have each person write down the name of someone whose help made a difference to them but who never got any credit.
Challenge everyone to thank that person by name before next week.

weeks.summary: Livingstone moves to the Bakwena, whose chief, Sechele, learns the alphabet on the first day, loves Isaiah, and asks why the gospel took so long to reach his ancestors. Sechele sends away all but his first wife in order to be baptised and is later suspended from communion, yet he keeps reading the Bible and preaches to his own people until he dies in 1892. The big idea: God doesn’t write people off after one stumble, and he works far beyond what we can see.

memory_verse.text: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

activity.title: Hard Questions
steps: Read aloud Sechele’s question about why no one had sent word to his ancestors sooner.
Give everyone a card and ask them to write, without their name, one hard question about God or faith they have wondered about.
Collect and shuffle the cards, then read a few aloud and talk about them together, without pressure to find neat answers.
Point out that Livingstone had no satisfying answer for Sechele, yet Sechele went on reading and seeking.
Offer to talk about any remaining questions with anyone privately after the session.

weeks.summary: Livingstone crosses the Kalahari to Lake Ngami, then takes his pregnant wife and small children on further journeys; a baby daughter dies, and on one trip the family goes four days without water. He reaches the Makololo, sees the slave trade for the first time, dreams of the Zambezi as a highway for honest trade, and sends Mary and the four children to Britain. The big idea: a big dream for God needs a second look when it costs the people closest to you without asking them.

memory_verse.text: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus.

activity.title: Who Pays the Cost?
steps: As a group, list a few big goals a teenager might chase: a sport, top grades, a band, a job, a ministry.
For each one, name who else pays part of the cost, such as parents giving lifts, siblings missing out or friends left behind.
Recall Mary Moffat’s fierce letter from the chapter and ask: was she right, and why didn’t Livingstone change course?
Have each person write down privately one plan or habit of theirs that costs someone close to them.
Encourage them to ask that person about it this week and to listen without defending themselves.

weeks.summary: A Boer commando attacks Sechele’s people, kills many and carries off women and children, and Livingstone’s house at Kolobeng is plundered. Sechele sets out to ask Queen Victoria for help, fails, and rebuilds his town himself, while in Britain Mary drifts, lonely and often ill, between rented rooms and the children grow up without a father. The big idea: God is a very present help in trouble, and he sees the hidden suffering that happens far from any battlefield.

memory_verse.text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.

activity.title: Hidden Loads
steps: Ask the group to name kinds of hardship that usually go unseen, such as caring for a sick relative, loneliness or money worries.
Discuss why the old biographies hurried past Mary’s suffering, and why this book insists on telling it.
Have each person privately write the name of one person in their life who may be carrying a hidden load.
Next to the name, have them write one practical thing they could do this week to make it lighter.
Close by praying silently for those people.

weeks.summary: Livingstone sets out for the Atlantic with twenty-seven men chosen by Sekeletu and led by Pitsane, through floods and fever, a strong-willed woman chief named Manenko, and a tense stand-off with the Chiboque. In Luanda he is offered a passage home but refuses, because he promised to bring the men back, and the ship he would have taken sinks. The big idea: God honours the one who keeps a promise even when it costs, though keeping faith with some people never excuses breaking it with others.

memory_verse.text: Who swears to his own hurt and does not change.

activity.title: The Promise Line
steps: Mark an imaginary line across the room, with “Must keep it” at one end and “Should break it” at the other.
Read out a few situations one at a time: you promised to help a friend but a better invitation comes up; you agreed to babysit and now feel unwell; you promised to keep a secret that now worries you.
For each, have everyone stand where they think it belongs, and ask a few people to explain why.
Point out that a secret that worries you, especially about someone’s safety, is one to take to a trusted adult.
Ask: Livingstone kept faith with twenty-seven men but left his wife alone. How can we keep promises to some people and forget the ones at home?

weeks.summary: The twenty-seven men come home as heroes, and Livingstone heads east with more than a hundred of Sekeletu’s men and the guide Sekwebu, sees Mosi-oa-Tunya and names it after Queen Victoria. Facing a risky river crossing, he reads Jesus’ promise to be with his disciples always, calls it the word of a gentleman of the strictest honour, and becomes calm; he reaches the Indian Ocean, but Sekwebu drowns on the voyage. The big idea: Jesus’ promise holds whether or not we feel it, and believing it comes before feeling calm.

memory_verse.text: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.

activity.title: Facts Before Feelings
steps: Ask everyone to think of something that makes them anxious, such as an exam, a hard conversation or a new place.
On one side of a sheet, have them write privately what they feel about it; on the other, what God has promised that is true regardless.
Read the chapter’s line “He didn’t feel calm and then believe. He believed, and then felt calm,” and talk about what it means.
Say Matthew 28:20 together slowly, twice.
Challenge everyone to say it the next time they are afraid this week, and then take one small step.

weeks.summary: Livingstone returns to Britain famous, resigns from the missionary society to lead a government expedition up the Zambezi, and tells Cambridge students, “I never made a sacrifice.” The expedition is blocked by the Kebrabasa rapids, which he had missed by walking round them, yet he won’t admit the mistake, and he treats colleagues such as Thomas Baines unfairly. The big idea: perseverance can be faith, but it can also be pride, and sometimes the brave thing is to say “I was wrong.”

memory_verse.text: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us.

activity.title: Faith or Pride?
steps: Read out a few short situations: a player who won’t quit a losing team; a student who won’t accept a teacher’s correction; someone who keeps praying for a friend for years; a person who won’t apologise because they were “basically right.”
For each, have the group vote thumbs up for “faithful perseverance” or thumbs down for “stubborn pride,” then talk about the votes.
Ask: what was Livingstone’s Kebrabasa moment, and what would admitting it have cost him?
Discuss who paid the cost of his calling, and whether calling it “no sacrifice” was fair to them.
Give everyone a quiet moment to think of one time they were wrong and haven’t admitted it, and to decide whether to put it right this week.

weeks.summary: Livingstone reaches Lake Nyasa, and with Bishop Mackenzie frees eighty-four captives at Mbame’s village; among the children freed in those weeks is a boy named Chuma. A deadly clash with raiders and Mackenzie’s lonely death from fever follow, and in April 1862 Mary dies at Shupanga, leaving Livingstone shattered. The big idea: the Lord is near the brokenhearted, and grief that honestly sees its own part can lead us to put things right.

memory_verse.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

activity.title: Two Kinds of Sorry
steps: Draw two columns headed “Feeling bad” and “Making it right.”
As a group, list what each looks like: for example, avoiding someone compared with naming what you did and apologising.
Ask: why does the chapter say it would be cruel to blame Livingstone for Mary’s death, but dishonest to say nothing about his choices?
Have each person privately write down one person they may have hurt and one step to make it right.
Pray silently, asking God for the courage to take that step.

weeks.summary: Drought and slave raids ruin the Shire valley, the government recalls the expedition, and Livingstone sails his small steamer to Bombay rather than let it be used in the slave trade. His eldest son Robert dies in an American prison camp, his mother dies, and he returns to Africa for the last time to seek the Nile’s source and expose the slave routes; when porters steal his medicine chest he feels he has received the sentence of death, but goes on. The big idea: like Abraham, faith sometimes means going on without knowing where the road leads.

memory_verse.text: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.

activity.title: A Letter Home
steps: Reread the paragraph about Robert and ask what he might have wanted from his father.
Talk about why it can be hard to say important things to parents or older relatives.
Give everyone five quiet minutes to draft, for their own eyes, a short letter to a parent, older relative or another adult who cares for them, naming one thing they are grateful for.
Let each person decide privately whether to send it, keep it, or pray about it first.

weeks.summary: In Manyema, crippled by ulcers and cared for by Susi, Chuma and Gardner, Livingstone reads the Bible through four times, then watches traders massacre hundreds of people at the market in Nyangwe. His account helps close the Zanzibar slave market, though modern imaging of his diary shows he was closer to the traders than his published version admitted; then Henry Morton Stanley finds him at Ujiji and saves his life. The big idea: we can bring God an honest “how long?” about evil, and then do the small thing that is ours to do.

memory_verse.text: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you “Violence!” and you will not save?

activity.title: Lament and Act
steps: Explain that a lament is an honest prayer of complaint to God, like Habakkuk’s “how long?”
As a group, name an injustice in the world today that makes people feel helpless, keeping to world events rather than personal stories.
Have each person write a short lament of three lines: what is wrong, how they feel about it, and what they ask God to do.
Add a fourth line: one small thing they could do, such as giving, writing or speaking up.
Invite anyone who wishes to read theirs aloud; no one has to.

weeks.summary: Carried through the Bangweulu swamps, Livingstone dies at Chitambo’s village, found, by his companions’ account, kneeling by his bed. Led by Susi and Chuma, the men bury his heart under a tree and carry his body and papers about a thousand miles to the coast, and Jacob Wainwright walks among the pallbearers at Westminster Abbey. The big idea: like a grain of wheat, a faithful life bears fruit after it is gone, often through people who receive little credit.

memory_verse.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

activity.title: Faithful Hands
steps: Read the words on Livingstone’s grave, “Brought by faithful hands over land and sea,” and ask whose hands they were.
As a group, list the African names that have appeared through this book, such as Mebalwe, Sechele, Pitsane, Manenko, Sekwebu, Susi, Chuma and Jacob Wainwright.
Talk about how the book’s honesty changes the way you see Livingstone, and what each person most wants to remember from his story.
Have each person write the name of one person who quietly serves in their church or school, and plan to thank them this week.
Close by praying for the grace to be faithful when no one is watching.
